author: Dan Antonelli
title: Yes, the graphic accompanying this post was made with AI. That’s the point.
content: Yes, the graphic accompanying this post was made with AI. That’s the point. Recently my buddy Kevin Marron of Blue Collar Millionaire ran a contest to pick the best logo among his FB community. He asked me and a few of our teammates to pick our favorites from more than 900 submissions. I expected there to be a pretty wide range of them - from good to bad, amateur to professional. What I didn’t expect was how many were clearly built with AI. I’d estimate more than half. And some were painfully obvious. As business owners, we all have to do the best we can with our marketing budget. Some simply don’t have the resources or knowledge yet to build a professional brand, and AI may be a short-term bridge until they can make that investment. But what if using AI for your logo or advertising is actually turning potential customers off? And yes, I totally get the obvious bias here. I run a branding agency. It would clearly be in my best interest and every designer’s best interest to tell you not to use AI. But some very recent research tells an interesting (and unbiased) story. A June 2026 Harris Poll/Cannes Lions study found that 78% of consumers feel AI makes advertising less authentic, 63% are less likely to buy from brands using AI-generated ads, and 54% are annoyed by the constant saturation of AI in marketing. Now, the study was about ads, not logos. But let’s face it, a lot of AI logos are becoming almost as obvious as the AI flyers and ads we’re all probably sick of seeing. Like the silly one in this post. And worth noting: an illustrated or mascot-based logo isn't automatically AI-generated. There's a big difference between prompting a tool for an image and having an illustrator develop an original character through strategy, sketching and refinement. One is generated. The other is intentionally built for a specific business. The 63% number is the one that really caught my attention. If 63% of consumers are less likely to buy from brands using AI-generated advertising, how much are you really saving by not hiring a professional? Or maybe the better question is: What’s the true cost of looking inauthentic and losing the trust of the people who already mistrust most contractors? Just something to think about, from a guy who admittedly runs a branding agency. So yeah, totally fair if you want to ignore me. All good 🙂 We’re still incredibly busy building brands the old-fashioned way. PS- The link to the study is below👇

author: Magazine 30.30 .eg
title: Faris Waked: From Business Administration to Building a Career in Design
content: Faris Waked: From Business Administration to Building a Career in Design At 26, Faris Waked from Dakahlia, Egypt, holds a degree in Business Administration from the Faculty of Commerce. During his final year of university, he specialized in Business Administration, building a strong academic foundation in a field that would remain part of his professional life even as his interests gradually shifted toward design. His academic background introduced him to areas such as marketing and branding, which helped him understand the connection between design, business, and the way brands communicate with their audiences. Today, Faris continues to work remotely as an accountant with a friend, drawing on his ability and background in accounting while simultaneously developing his career in design. Rather than completely abandoning his original field, he has chosen to maintain that professional connection while pursuing the creative direction he has built over the years. A Self-Taught Beginning Faris's interest in design began around the start of university, and possibly even earlier, when he started experimenting with simple designs using PicsArt. During his university years, he continued learning on his own, although not always consistently. He would explore new tools, experiment with different ideas, and work on simple projects, many of which remained unfinished. His learning process gradually expanded into different areas of digital production. He initially explored Premiere Pro, then moved to Illustrator and Photoshop. Over time, he realized that design appealed to him more than video editing, leading him to focus increasingly on the field. Much of his learning came through YouTube, while he also tried to find people with more experience who could guide him and help him better understand the profession. September 2024: From Learning to Professional Practice A major step came after his military service, when Faris joined an internship at an online company. The experience gave him a clearer understanding of how professional work actually operates beyond tutorials and personal projects. In September 2024, he joined his first agency. Having someone around him to learn from and receive guidance from made a significant difference. It helped him understand the practical side of design and how creative work is handled in a professional environment. The experience also introduced him to the realities of working with clients: deadlines, revisions, changing requirements, and the need to understand exactly what a client is looking for before delivering a final design. Keeping Two Professional Paths Open After graduation, Faris continued working remotely as an accountant with a friend while developing his design career. He did not want to leave his existing work immediately without knowing whether design could become a sustainable professional path. Instead, he chose to test the possibility gradually. He would finish his work and dedicate another two to three hours to learning, practicing, and applying what he was learning in design. That approach allowed him to develop his skills without making an immediate and uncertain career decision. Over time, as his abilities improved and people around him became aware of his work, he began taking on paid design projects. For Faris, maintaining both areas has become part of the process: accounting remains a field in which he is capable and comfortable, while design represents the creative direction he has deliberately built for himself. From a First Paid Project to International Clients One of his early paid projects came through people close to him, including a dental clinic owned by his cousins. It was a small but meaningful step because it marked the transition from learning and experimenting to providing design work for an actual client. As his experience grew, so did the scale of his work. He began working on larger projects and eventually took on freelance opportunities with companies and clients outside Egypt, including clients from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Jordan, Iraq, and other markets. These experiences helped him develop a deeper understanding of professional design. He learned that the job is not simply about knowing how to use software. It also requires communication, understanding a client's needs, handling feedback, working under pressure, and delivering the right solution within the required timeframe. The Challenge Was Not Just Learning Design For Faris, one of the biggest challenges was entering a new field while already working in another. There was always uncertainty about whether the new direction would actually work, while balancing a professional commitment with continuous learning required discipline. Another challenge was the lack of a mentor during the early stages. Much of his learning depended on self-study, experimentation, and searching for people who could help him understand the field from a professional perspective. Once he began working professionally, the challenges changed. Deadlines, pressure, revisions, and client requests became part of the learning process. Through these experiences, Faris came to understand that professional design involves much more than mastering software. It is about communication, understanding requirements, solving visual problems, and delivering work that serves its intended purpose. You Do Not Have to Know the Destination From the Start Faris believes that people do not necessarily need to know exactly where they are going when they begin learning something new. His advice is to start with something you genuinely enjoy, even if it is not your primary field of work. Finding a mentor, speaking with experienced people, and being willing to admit that you still have more to learn can make the process easier. There is also no need to wait for perfect circumstances before starting. By learning, experimenting, and gaining real experience, people can gradually discover whether a field is truly right for them. For Faris, the process was not about abandoning one career overnight and choosing another. It was about giving himself the opportunity to explore design seriously, build real skills, gain professional experience, and eventually recognize that it was a direction worth continuing. By Haneen Awaga

author: Hayden Williams Illustrations
title: 🚫 AI - Hand Drawn Only
content: 🚫 AI - Hand Drawn Only As a self-taught fashion illustrator who has been fortunate to be successful for 15+ years, I’ve gone from creating using traditionally mediums, to drawing digitally & continuing to evolve at my own pace. I’ve been able to maintain longevity and continue to make an impact without compromising my craft. Fashion illustration is already a hugely under appreciated part of the fashion industry, so the recent heavy reliance on AI generated art is incredibly disheartening. I’m seeing people claim to be artists & fashion illustrators using prompts to create their work. Even luxury fashion labels are starting to choose AI generated fashion illustrations over hiring fashion illustrators with genuine skill and craftsmanship. Personally, I feel like it’s lazy and dilutes the purpose of being an artist to begin with. I’d feel like a fraud in the comments, accepting praise for something that a computer made. To me, AI-generated fashion illustration is often easy to spot. It can create the illusion of a hand drawn sketch but is entirely done by a computer, and it ultimately makes the work feel less distinctive. More importantly, it takes opportunities away from real illustrators who may not have the same visibility/platform as me & that rely on their craft for a living. It also is raising serious concerns about AI using artists work without consent. So, this is simply an encouragement to keep creating with your hands. There’s nothing more inspiring than seeing genuine skill, individuality and artistry on display. That human to human connection with creativity is something AI can try to imitate, but can never replace and will always be superior! #FashionIllustration #DigitalArt #AI
